Thought: I'll evaluate each substance based on its typical flash point:

A. Fuel oil - Typically has a flash point above 60°C, so it wouldn't form explosive mixtures at 21°C.

B. Gasoline - Has a flash point around -43°C, which is well below 21°C, so it can form explosive mixtures at room temperature.

C. Nitro thinner - Contains nitrocellulose and solvents with very low flash points, typically below 21°C.

D. Petroleum - This is a broad term, but crude petroleum typically has a flash point above 21°C.

E. Synthetic resin lacquers - These typically contain solvents with low flash points, often below 21°C.

F. Acetone - Has a flash point of approximately -20°C, which is below 21°C, so it can form explosive mixtures at room temperature.

G. Turpentine substitute - Typically has a flash point around 30-40°C, which is above 21°C.

Based on this analysis, the substances that can form explosive mixtures at room temperature (up to 21°C) are: B (Gasoline), C (Nitro thinner), E (Synthetic resin lacquers), and F (Acetone).
